What Is a Gilt? UK Gilts Explained + Tax Calculator

A gilt is a bond issued by the UK government through the Debt Management Office (DMO). A conventional gilt pays a fixed coupon (interest) twice a year on each £100 of nominal value and repays £100 at its maturity date. Gilts trade on the market, so their price moves – mainly with interest rates. If you sell before maturity you could get back less than you paid; if you hold to maturity you receive £100 per £100 nominal.

When you're tricked into sending a bank transfer to a fraudster. Since 7 October 2024, banks must usually reimburse eligible UK Faster Payments and CHAPS victims up to £85,000 per claim.

How Money Works in the UK, Explained in Pictures

Money is anything people trust to pay for things , to measure prices (a pound is a ruler for value) and to save for later . Today almost all of it is just numbers in bank accounts. Notes and coins are a small slice. The Bank of England's 2014 paper Money creation in the modern economy found that bank deposits made up about 97% of the money in circulation at the time, with notes and coins only about 3%. Money's three jobs.
2Banks create most money when they lend
How Money Works in the UK, Explained in Pictures

When a bank gives you a loan, it doesn't hand over someone else's savings. It simply types new money into your account. The loan is the bank's asset and your new deposit is new money. In the Bank of England's words, whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit . When you repay a loan, that money disappears again. Banks can't create money without limit: they're held back by how many people want to borrow, by rules on safety, and by interest rates. A new loan creates a new deposit.
3The Bank of England and Bank Rate
How Money Works in the UK, Explained in Pictures

The Bank of England is the UK's central bank. Its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets Bank Rate , the interest rate it pays banks on the money they hold with it. Bank Rate influences what banks charge for loans and pay on savings. Bank Rate is 4.00% , as at 5 November 2026, and has been since 5 November 2026. Bank Rate is 4.00% (since 5 November 2026).

The government pays for schools, hospitals and pensions with taxes. When it spends more than it collects, it borrows by selling gilts : IOUs that pay interest and repay £100 at the end. The Debt Management Office (DMO) sells them for the Treasury. Buyers include pension funds and insurers (who need steady, long-term income), banks, overseas investors and, during quantitative easing, the Bank of England. The DMO's data shows about £2.94 trillion of gilts in issue (nominal, including inflation uplift on index-linked gilts) at close of business on 9 October 2026. Gilts: the government's IOUs.

Quantitative easing (QE) : when cutting Bank Rate wasn't enough, the Bank of England created new money (central bank reserves) and used it to buy gilts and some corporate bonds. That pushed down long-term interest rates to support spending. The total reached £895 billion (£875 billion of gilts and £20 billion of corporate bonds) by the end of 2021, held in the Asset Purchase Facility (APF). Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse: since 2022 the Bank has been letting gilts mature and selling some. By September 2026 the APF had fallen to around £488 billion . The calculator’s own note says charging losses are ignored. E.ON Next’s guide says some of the electricity you are billed for is lost as heat and in battery warming, from around 10% to 25% depending on the charger, cable and weather. The cost per mile article shows how an assumed 10% loss changes the sum, from 9.3p to about 10.4p per mile at 32.69p/kWh. That is one supplier’s guide, so treat the range as a rough guide.

The calculator uses one figure for miles per kWh. Which? says in its 2022 article that weather, driving style and speed all affect an electric car’s range, and that you get fewer miles on a motorway than around town. Its tests found real range averaged 18% below the official figure. A lower miles-per-kWh figure raises the cost per mile directly, since the sum is price ÷ miles per kWh. For example, 3.0 miles per kWh instead of 3.5 at 32.69p gives about 10.9p per mile rather than 9.3p. E.ON Next also notes that in cold weather more energy goes into warming the battery.

If you do not already have one, the Energy Saving Trust gives the typical cost of installing a home charge point as around £800 to £1,200 (page last updated 25 March 2025). It also says you need off-street parking, and typically a smart meter and a suitable tariff to get the most from it. The calculator’s home rate does not include this one-off cost.

According to GOV.UK’s rate tables, a zero-emission car pays £10 when it is first registered. From the second payment onward, electric cars pay the standard rate of £200 for 12 months. An electric car with a list price of more than £50,000 can pay an extra £440 a year for five years (from the second time it is taxed). Check GOV.UK’s table for which registration dates and prices are affected.

GOV.UK’s page on Electric Vehicle Excise Duty (updated 28 October 2026) says that from 1 April 2028 a mileage-based charge will apply to electric cars: 3p per mile for battery-electric cars and 1.5p per mile for plug-in hybrids, rising with CPI from 2029 to 2030. It says primary legislation will be introduced, so it is not law until Parliament passes it, and the details could change. Illustration, if it goes ahead as announced (hypothetical use).
